newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia oilmen meet Congress in strike countdown.
newsitem.headline: Colombia oilmen meet Congress in strike countdown.

text.p: The heads of Colombia's main oil workers' union met lawmakers Wednesday as the countdown started to an all-out strike in the state-run oil sector.
In the meeting which began shortly before 1000 local/1500 GMT, labor leaders and members of a congressional committee were due to discuss government plans to carve up the state oil company Ecopetrol.
The Mines and Energy Ministry has submitted a bill to Congress proposing that natural gas operations be hived off from Ecopetrol and managed by an independent company to be called Ecogas.

The 7,000-strong USO union, however, said it would only accept the plan if Ecogas was set up as a subsidiary and directly managed by Ecopetrol. It fears that the creation of an autonomous company would mark the start of the break-up of Ecopetrol and a possible halfway house on the road to eventual privatization.
"We're meeting with members of a congressional committee this morning for an exchange of opinions," Gustavo Triana, member of the USO national executive, told Reuters.

"But we do not accept that the government has nothing to do with the bill to create Ecogas. This has been a way for the Mines and Energy Minister (Rodrigo Villamizar) to wash his hands of the matter," he added.
A top-level meeting between Villamizar and the USO leaders broke up in acrimony Tuesday evening after Interior Minister Horacio Serpa, who had called the meeting, failed to show up.
That prompted USO leader Hernando Hernandez to say that a long-threatened oil workers strike would begin "from that moment".
Triana said preparations had begun to gradually wind down refining and production operations but did not say when a total stoppage would begin.
An Ecopetrol spokesman said Serpa was due to telephone Hernandez later this morning in a bid to kick-start talks to avert a strike.
But in comments to reporters Wednesday, Ecopetrol chief Antonio Urdinola indicated there was little margin for negotiation.

"It's up to Congress to find a solution that resolves this dilemma and gives the government what it wants, which is the total independence and autonomy of Ecogas and calms USO fears that this will be the beginning of the end for Ecopetrol," Urdinola said.
"Ecopetrol cannot assume either the investment or the responsibility for supplying gas pipelines to the whole country...that is work that needs state funds for a long time," he said.
In the event of a strike, Urdinola said non-unionized personnel would be able to run essential operations for three to four weeks and could guarantee fuel supplies for that period.
But according to USO figures, fuel supplies for the capital Bogota would last just eight days and those in Cali, Colombia's second largest city, would last for just two days, Triana said.
